hints: Look separately at the left benzene ring with OH, the central -NH-C=O link, and the right C=C in the side chain.
walkthrough:
Break capsaicin into three reactive zones**
Look left to right. On the left you have -OH directly attached to a benzene ring, that is a phenol, not just an alcohol. In the middle you have -NH-C=O, that is an amide link. On the right side chain you have C=C, that is an alkene. The $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ group is told to ignore.
Final answer: phenol, amide and alkene (C=C). All three needed.

hints: Recall what excess $\text{Br}_2$(aq) in the dark does to a phenol ring separately from what it does to an isolated C=C.
Think about how many $\text{Br}_2$ molecules are consumed in total and what small molecule is lost when Br substitutes on the ring.
Check that Br atoms balance: addition to C=C adds two Br with no by-product, while ring substitution releases $\text{HBr}$.
walkthrough:
Separate the two different bromination modes**
In the dark there is no free radical substitution. The phenol ring is highly activated by the -OH group, so it undergoes electrophilic substitution. The isolated alkene in the side chain undergoes electrophilic addition. They happen independently.

Place the three Br atoms**
For the phenol, only one free ortho/para position remains highly reactive because one ortho position is blocked by $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ and para is blocked by the $\text{CH}_2\text{NHCO}$ side chain. So one Br substitutes ortho to OH. For the alkene, $\text{Br}_2$ adds across the double bond, giving -CHBr-CHBr-. That is three Br atoms in total on the organic product.

Balance the equation**
Addition to the alkene uses one whole $\text{Br}_2$ with nothing lost. Substitution on the ring uses a second $\text{Br}_2$ but loses H as $\text{HBr}$. So: $$\text{capsaicin} + 2\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{tribromo-product} + \text{HBr}$$

Final answer: capsaicin + $2\text{Br}_2$ -> tribromo organic product + $\text{HBr}$
Organic product: capsaicin with one Br on phenol ring ortho to OH (para to $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$) and one Br on each carbon of the former side-chain C=C.

hints: Recall what $\text{H}_2$/Pt does to benzene and to an isolated alkene when used in excess with heat.
Decide which groups survive: phenol OH, $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ and amide remain unchanged under these conditions.
walkthrough:
Reduce the aromatic ring**
You are told the six membered ring reacts like benzene. With excess $\text{H}_2$ and Pt with heat, benzene adds $3\text{H}_2$ to give cyclohexane. So draw a saturated cyclohexane ring with the same three substituents in the same positions: $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$-, HO- and -$\text{CH}_2\text{NHCO}$-.

Reduce the alkene**
The side chain C=C also adds one $\text{H}_2$ to give $\text{CH}_2$-$\text{CH}_2$. The amide C=O is not reduced by $\text{H}_2$/Pt under these conditions, so the -$\text{NH}$-$\text{C=O}$- link stays intact.

Final answer: Product with benzene ring reduced to cyclohexane (retaining $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$, HO and $\text{CH}_2\text{NHCO}$ substituents) and side-chain C=C reduced to $\text{CH}_2$-$\text{CH}_2$ to give saturated $-\text{(CH}_2)_6\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ tail.

hints: Note the product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{COOH}$ must come from cleavage of the side chain C=C to give a carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
Link cleavage to vigorous oxidation**
To cut a C=C and oxidise both ends fully to carboxylic acids you need very vigorous oxidation, not cold dilute conditions which would give a diol. That is hot and concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$, which cleaves the $\text{-CH=CH-CH(CH}_3)_2$ end to give $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$.
Final answer: hot, concentrated, acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ / $\text{KMnO}_4$. All three conditions needed.

hints: Use Table 8.1 to match each environment: $\text{CH}_3$ alkane, CH next to C=O, and $\text{COOH}$ acid proton.
Apply the n+1 rule by counting equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon for $\text{CH}_3$ and CH.
Remember why the $\text{COOH}$ proton is a singlet with no splitting from neighbours.
walkthrough:
Assign chemical shifts from the table**
The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are simple alkane protons, so $\delta$ 0.9-1.7. The CH is alkyl next to C=O ($\text{>CH-C=O}$), so $\delta$ 2.2-3.0. The acid proton $\text{RCOOH}$ is strongly deshielded, so $\delta$ 9.0-13.0.

Predict splitting with n+1**
Splitting comes from protons on the adjacent carbon only. Each $\text{CH}_3$ sees 1 proton on the CH next door, so n = 1 gives doublet (1+1 = 2). The CH sees 6 equivalent protons from the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so n = 6 gives 7 lines, a septet, often just called a multiplet.

Explain the acid singlet**
The $\text{COOH}$ proton has no vicinal protons on the adjacent carbonyl carbon and undergoes rapid exchange, so it is not split and appears as a singlet.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3$: $\delta$ 0.9-1.7, doublet, split by 1 H on neighbouring CH / one vicinal proton.
CH: $\delta$ 2.2-3.0, multiplet / heptet / septet, split by 6 H on neighbouring $2 \times \text{CH}_3$ / six vicinal protons.
COOH: $\delta$ 9.0-13.0, singlet.

hints: Hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ hydrolyses the amide link: think amine plus carboxylate, and also deprotonates the phenol.
Use the given formulae $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{10}\text{NO}_2\text{Na}$ for H and $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{17}\text{O}_2\text{Na}$ for K to check which fragment keeps nitrogen.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the amide**
Hot $\text{NaOH}$ breaks -$\text{NH-CO}$- into -$\text{NH}_2$ plus -$\text{COO}^-$. So the left benzyl fragment becomes an amine, and the right acyl fragment becomes a carboxylate salt. The C=C in the acid tail is untouched by $\text{NaOH}$.

Also neutralise the phenol**
Phenol is acidic enough to react with $\text{NaOH}$ to give $\text{ArO}^- \text{Na}^+$. The $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ ether does not react. So H contains both -$\text{NH}_2$ and -$\text{O}^- \text{Na}^+$, matching $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{10}\text{NO}_2\text{Na}$, while K is the $\text{C}_{10}$ sodium carboxylate.

Final answer: H: $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$-$\text{C}_6\text{H}_3$(O^- Na^+)-$\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ (sodium phenoxide of benzylamine).
K: $\text{Na}^+$ ^-OOC-$\text{(CH}_2)_4$-CH=CH-CH($\text{CH}_3)_2$ (sodium carboxylate, alkene retained).

hints: Identify one term for breaking the amide with water and alkali, and a second term for forming $\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ salts.
walkthrough:
Name the two processes**
Splitting the amide by hot aqueous alkali is hydrolysis. Converting the phenol -OH and the formed carboxylic acid to their sodium salts is neutralisation, which is an acid-base reaction.
Final answer: hydrolysis and neutralisation / acid-base.

hints: Recall that $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether reduces the amide C=O to $\text{CH}_2$ but leaves C=C, phenol and ether unchanged.
walkthrough:
Reduce only the amide carbonyl**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a powerful reducing agent that converts -$\text{NH-C=O}$- to -$\text{NH-CH}_2$-. Picture the carbonyl oxygen removed as water on work up and replaced by two H atoms. Everything else stays the same: the phenol OH, the $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ group and the side chain C=C are all retained, giving a secondary amine L.

Final answer: L: $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$-$\text{C}_6\text{H}_3$(OH)-$\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{(CH}_2)_4$CH=CH-CH($\text{CH}_3)_2$ (amide C=O reduced to $\text{CH}_2$, secondary amine, alkene retained).
